functional_compartments.function_note: Unusually long fascicles for a forearm muscle, an architecture suited to its role generating elbow flexion velocity across a wide range of forearm rotation rather than pure force.

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Two approaches. Arm compartment: transverse on the anterolateral arm about 2-3 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle. Forearm compartment: transverse on the anterolateral forearm about 2-3 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: In the arm, superficial to brachialis over the radial cortex. In the forearm, the most superficial of four muscles over the radial cortex -- supinator deepest, then extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor carpi radialis longus, then brachioradialis.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: To tell brachioradialis from extensor carpi radialis longus, ask for wrist extension and abduction with the forearm pronated.
structures_at_risk: posterior interosseous nerve (between the heads of supinator, in the forearm window)
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: The two compartments correspond to the muscle's two arborization zones. The source names the intermuscular fascia between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus as a concrete source of error for less experienced injectors in the forearm window.

trigger_points.location_description: Proximal belly, one to three fingerbreadths distal to the elbow crease over the muscle mass on the radial forearm.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Lateral epicondyle, the radial dorsal forearm and wrist, and the dorsal web of the thumb; a painful handshake and aching at the radial wrist and thumb web are the typical complaints.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Sustained gripping with the elbow flexed and the forearm in mid-position (carrying, hammering, racquet sports, hand-shaking jobs), repetitive elbow flexion under load; associated with extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, supinator and extensor digitorum trigger points.
trigger_points.notes: Active brachioradialis trigger points reproduced the presenting pain in 10 of 20 patients with lateral epicondylalgia (Fernandez-Carnero et al. 2007). Non-myofascial differential: lateral epicondyle tendinosis, radial tunnel syndrome, Wartenberg's syndrome, intersection syndrome, De Quervain's disease, C6 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 34; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 34, pp. 329-342 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: A flexor of the elbow whose leverage is best with the forearm midway between pronation and supination, and which is recruited especially for rapid movements and against resistance (Gray's; EMG of Basmajian). From a supinated or pronated position it rotates the forearm back toward neutral but is not a prime rotator beyond that. Its small cross-sectional area (the smallest of the elbow crossers in Murray's series, ~1.2 cm²) is offset by the longest fascicles (~18 cm) and a large flexion moment arm, giving a large excursion and a moment-generating capacity out of proportion to its size; it contributes ~19% of flexion torque. MacConaill classified it as a "shunt" muscle whose line of pull compresses the joint during fast flexion; the shunt/spurt dichotomy is contested but the joint-compressive component is real. Grip with the elbow flexed loads the muscle isometrically, which is why handshake and jar-opening provoke its TrPs.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None intrinsic. Distally, the crossing with APL/EPB may develop an adventitial bursa (intersection syndrome). Adjacent structures and relations: The radial nerve and its terminal division lie deep to the muscle at the elbow; the superficial branch of the radial nerve runs beneath it and emerges between its tendon and ECRL about 8–9 cm proximal to the styloid; the radial artery lies under its medial edge for most of the forearm, the muscle forming the "lateral wall" of Henry's approach.

trigger_points.location: Belly of the muscle in the proximal third of the forearm, a few centimetres distal to the lateral epicondyle, palpated by pincer grip against the underlying ECRL.
trigger_points.referred_pain: lateral epicondyle and lateral elbow, down the dorsal-radial forearm, to the dorsal web space between thumb and index (and the base of the thumb).
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: "Tennis elbow" pain, painful handshake, weak grip, dropping objects; thumb-web pain resembling superficial radial neuropathy. In patients with lateral epicondylalgia, manual examination reproduced the lateral elbow pain from brachioradialis TrPs in 50% (Fernández-Carnero 2007). Entrapment: Not attributed to brachioradialis TrPs; the superficial radial nerve is compressed between brachioradialis and ECRL tendons in pronation (Wartenberg syndrome) as a separate entity. Associated TrPs: ECRL, ECRB, supinator, extensor digitorum, triceps medial head.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 34, Hand extensor and brachioradialis muscles; ch. 33 pain guide.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: triceps (TrP2 in the medial head, TrP1 spill)
supraspinatus (its pattern concentrates on the lateral epicondyle)
infraspinatus and scalenes (radial forearm and thumb)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO the lateral elbow / radial forearm from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Preferred donor for tendon transfer to flexor pollicis longus (tetraplegia) and for radial-side grafts; guide to the superficial radial nerve and radial artery in volar approaches to the distal radius; tenderness here in "resistant tennis elbow" should prompt examination of the radial tunnel.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.

tests.name: Trigger-point examination
tests.performance: Palpation of taut bands in brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB, ED and supinator
tests.positive_finding: Reproduction of the presenting lateral elbow pain
tests.accuracy: Referred pain reproduced the presenting pain in 50–70% of patients with lateral epicondylalgia (Fernández-Carnero 2007)
tests.source: Fernández-Carnero J, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, de la Llave-Rincón AI, Ge HY, Arendt-Nielsen L. Prevalence of and referred pain from myofascial trigger points in the forearm muscles in patients with lateral epicondylalgia. Clin J Pain. 2007;23(4):353–360.

clinical.tests_caveat: Values are taken from the cited primary studies. Most series are small and reference standards differ (surgery, arthroscopy, electrodiagnostics), so treat the numbers as indicative. The systematic review of Zwerus et al. (2018) found 24 described elbow tests, only 14 with any accuracy data, and concluded that no single test can rule an elbow diagnosis in or out on its own. Where no accuracy data exist, this is stated rather than estimated.

(2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Elbow flexion: electromyographically a reserve flexor, most active in rapid flexion and flexion against load, and strongest with the forearm in mid-position (semiprone); its line of pull along the forearm gives it a joint-compressing "shunt" character in fast movements [59] [grade B] [5]. Minor: Weak rotation of the forearm toward neutral from full pronation or full supination [1, 5]. Wrist: No wrist crossing (insertion is proximal to the joint), so it has no direct wrist action; it is, however, a deforming force on radial styloid fragments in distal radius fractures and is sometimes released during fixation [grade B] [4]. Importance: A prime transfer donor because it is proximally innervated and expendable: BR to FPL for key pinch in tetraplegia, BR to ECRB and other rebalancing transfers [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: None. Coupled structures: Radial nerve and its superficial branch, ECRL (Wartenberg interval, intersection region distally), radial styloid, cephalic vein territory superficially [1, 36].

trigger_points.location: Proximal belly, one to three fingerbreadths distal to the elbow crease over the muscle mass on the radial forearm (chapter 34) [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Lateral epicondyle, the radial dorsal forearm and wrist, and the dorsal web of the thumb; a painful handshake and aching at the radial wrist and thumb web are the typical complaints [2, 3, 34].
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Sustained gripping with the elbow flexed and the forearm in mid-position (carrying, hammering, racquet sports, hand-shaking jobs), repetitive elbow flexion under load; associated with ECRL, ECRB, supinator and EDC trigger points [2, 3, 34].

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into BR territory (radial forearm, radial wrist, thumb web)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: Lateral epicondyle tendinosis, radial tunnel syndrome, Wartenberg's syndrome, intersection syndrome, De Quervain's disease, C6 radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: In radial nerve palsy BR is examined first and recovers first after spiral-groove lesions. Wartenberg's syndrome is compression of the superficial radial nerve where it emerges between the BR and ECRL tendons, aggravated by pronation [36]. Active BR trigger points reproduced the presenting pain in 10 of 20 patients with lateral epicondylalgia [34].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
